newsitem.title: USA: Wall Street faces choppy trade.
newsitem.headline: Wall Street faces choppy trade.

text.p: Wall Street is heading into week of further choppy trading, but soothed of fears of an imminent interest rate hike.

Federal Reseve Chairman Alan Greenspan spoke last week and calmed investors, reassuring them he was not trying to talk stock prices lower, and the February employment report on Friday turned out to be a boon for markets.
This week, the market has little to take its cue from until Friday when the February producer price index and capacity utilization and industrial production data are released, analysts said.

"I think we are in for a multi-swing week," said Phil Roth, chief technical analyst at Dean Witter Reynolds. "The positive is that the trend is still up. The negative is that the market is overbought in the medium-term and will not be able to sustain a run. It will be a choppy week."

Last week's trading was marked by broad swings, with the Dow industrials down 66 on Tuesday and up 93 on Wednesdsay. The Dow ended Friday up 56 points at 7,001, posting a gain of 123 points for the week.

Wall Street received a boost last Friday from a February employment report that showed non-payrolls to be stronger than forecast while indicating little upward pressure on wages. Some analysts attributed the strength in payrolls to service jobs resulting from February's spell of mild weather.
The report eased the fear on Wall Street that the Federal Reserve would raise interest rates at the March 25 meeting of its policy-making Federal Open Market Committee.
"Worries about Fed tighteing are fading fast now that the employment report is out, and the PPI will help that," said Hugh Johnson, chief investment officer at First Albany Corp.
He said that softness in energy prices indicated that the PPI could either come in on target or lower.

The PPI is expected to drop by 0.1 percent, compared with a 0.3 percent drop in January while the core rate, which excludes food and energy prices, is expected to rise by 0.1 percent from an unchanged reading the previous month.

"It looks like it will be a positive week. The only thing that could hold us back is concern about valuations," Johnson said. "Whether you are talking about the techs in particular or stocks in general, many feel the market is overvalued."
He said that some groups have not participated in the move this year, including utilities and cyclical groups such as retailers, autos and some housing stocks.
Some money has started to move into the utilities, Johnson said, but their fundamentals remained tricky at best.
"There is a lot going on in terms of deregulation in the utility industry as well as a lot of capital spending to improve existing nuclear facilities," he said.
"Stock selection will be very important in this area. Every investors should make sure there is plenty of coverage of dividends."
